title: Collapse adjacent equal group keys before HT probe in hash aggregate sink
reasons: abandoned by the implementer after investigation
summary: I added a run-collapse fast path in GroupedAggregateHashTable::AddChunk, in src/execution/aggregate_hashtable.cpp only, with no header change. It runs after TryAddCompressedGroups and before the normal hash path. When every group column is fixed-width (TypeIsConstantSize) and there are at most 8 columns, it looks for runs of adjacent rows with identical keys. Two rows count as equal when both are NULL or both are valid with the same bytes (memcmp). If more than n/2 rows start a run, it bails out to the normal path. Otherwise it slices the run heads into dict_state.unique_values, hashes them, calls FindOrCreateGroups on the heads only, gives every row its run head's address and calls UpdateAggregates. It built cleanly and the bench checks passed. Measured: the subquery HASH_GROUP_BY CPU time went from 6.48s to 5.62s in the profile, but q18 wall time only moved 635->629 ms (-0.9%) in one run and 630->612 ms (-2.8%) in another. Both are inside the ~5% noise band and below the acceptance bar, so I am abandoning it.
notes: Cutting the probes by about 4x (only ~25% of rows are run heads on q18) does not change wall time much for a 15M-group aggregate. Hashing, probing and matching are not the bottleneck. The cost is most likely in creating and materialising 15M groups into the TupleDataCollection and in partition finalize/combine, which run collapse cannot touch. Follow-up for q18: get a breakdown of sink vs finalize for this aggregate and target the group materialisation or finalize/combine, for example a perfect-hash/direct-indexed aggregate for dense integer keys, like the q13 large perfect HA. The code is small and correct, so it could be revived later as a cheap helper for low-cardinality clustered aggregates, but by itself it has no measurable effect on q18.

title: In-place finalize: combine radix partitions without re-materializing first-seen groups
reasons: abandoned by the implementer after investigation
summary:
I implemented the in-place finalize and it builds and gives correct results, but it made q18 slightly slower instead of faster, so I'm abandoning it.

What I changed:
- Added GroupedAggregateHashTable::CombineInPlace. It scans the partition with KEEP_EVERYTHING_PINNED and builds a pointer table over the partition's own rows, using the same salt and linear-probing logic as FindOrCreateGroupsInternal. A first-seen row becomes the target (entry.SetPointer(source_row)) and is pushed to live_rows. A row that matches an existing group has its states combined into the target with one CombineStates call per chunk.
- In RadixHTLocalSourceState::Finalize, the in-place path is used only when the aggregate did not spill (!sink.external), the layout has no destructors, and the result is scanned once (DESTROY_AFTER_DONE). Otherwise the existing path runs.
- Scan gathers the group columns from live_rows in slices of up to STANDARD_VECTOR_SIZE, runs FinalizeStates, and resets the collection at the end.

I confirmed the path is taken with a temporary debug throw: 128 partitions of about 117K rows each, with only 6 duplicates in 117K. So about 15M appends, state inits and re-scans are skipped.

Measurements (repeated `dbe-tool sql` runs, same build with the path on and off):
- Isolated `SELECT count(*), sum(s) FROM (SELECT l_orderkey, sum(l_quantity) s FROM lineitem GROUP BY l_orderkey)`: about 600–620ms with the path on (excluding the first run) against 647–685ms off. That is within run-to-run noise.
- Full q18: 761–852ms on (about 805 on average) against 746–759ms off once warm. So about 5–7% slower.
- `bench q18` showed +17% to +30% with the path on, but also +13% with it off. The bench comparison against best is skewed for this build, so I relied on the on/off sql runs instead.
- The profiled HASH_GROUP_BY CPU time stayed at 4.60s, the same as the existing range.

Conclusion: copying groups again during finalize is not a meaningful part of the roughly 320ns per group. The cost is in the sink phase.
notes:
- The hypothesis is refuted. Even with nearly all 15M groups first seen in finalize, skipping the second append, state init and re-scan did not reduce aggregate CPU or wall time, and q18 got about 5% slower. Possible reasons: the whole partition stays pinned through the scan instead of blocks being freed as they are read, and the scan gathers through row pointers instead of reading sequentially.
- The per-group cost must be in the sink phase: thread-local HT inserts, abandon, and appending into partitioned data, including the 128-way partition split. The next idea should target that phase, for example fewer or cheaper materializations in the sink when the HT is abandoned.
- `dbe-tool bench` reported this build 13% slower than best even with the new path compiled out. When an effect is under about 10%, compare on and off with repeated `dbe-tool sql` runs of the same query instead of trusting bench against best.
- The working tree still contains the implementation, with the gate enabled, for the record.

title: Skip unpartitioned staging for fixed-width group layouts in hash aggregate sink
reasons: abandoned by the implementer after investigation
summary: I added `!layout_ptr->AllConstant()` to the staging condition in GroupedAggregateHashTable::FindOrCreateGroupsInternal. With it, fixed-width group layouts scatter straight into partitioned_data and skip the unpartitioned_data staging and the Repartition on Abandon. The build succeeded and results were correct. It gave no gain. `bench q18`: best 682.7 ms, mine 686.2 ms (+0.5%, within noise). On the isolated `SELECT max(s) FROM (SELECT l_orderkey, sum(l_quantity) s ... GROUP BY l_orderkey)`, warm runs were 610-700 ms before (one cold 980 ms, then 953, 698, 613, 698, 610) and 685-880 ms after (882, 712, 685, 805, 723, 746). So it is not faster and may be a little slower. I skipped the step 1 timers. The end-to-end on/off comparison already showed the staging path is not a cost worth removing.
notes: The other threshold (`< 2` instead of `<= 4` for fixed-width) sends q18's groups the same way, because about 512 new groups per chunk over 128 partitions is 4 per partition. So that variant was in effect tested too. For fixed-width rows, the stage-plus-repartition copy is not a significant part of the sink. This differs from the heap-layout result on q16 (-5%). Q18 sink cost must be elsewhere: hash probe and compare, InitializeStates, the aggregate update, or the scan. A perf or cycle-level breakdown of FindOrCreateGroupsInternal compared with UpdateAggregates is needed before trying another sink-side idea for q18. Runs of `dbe-tool sql` are noisy (±15%), so use bench for decisions.

title: Ablation-timed breakdown of radix agg sink per-group cost, then fix the top component
reasons: abandoned by the implementer after investigation
summary:
I stopped after the measurement step and am not submitting a change. No sink sub-step costs more than 8% on its own, and the step-2 fix the plan named, growing the local sink capacity, makes things about 30% slower.

The ablation code is temporary and must not be committed. It reads a flag from a session variable (`SET VARIABLE dbe_ablate=N`) in `src/execution/radix_partitioned_hashtable.cpp` and `src/execution/aggregate_hashtable.cpp`; the harness will reset the tree.

Test query: `SELECT max(s) FROM (SELECT l_orderkey k, sum(l_quantity) s FROM lineitem GROUP BY k)`, 15M groups, 8 threads, hot runs via `dbe-tool sql`. Timings are wall time; the machine is noisy (about ±5%, first run of each batch dropped).

| Variant | Wall time | Change |
|---|---|---|
| Baseline | ~455 ms | – |
| (a) skip sink InitializeStates | ~710 ms | slower (states left as garbage; tells us nothing) |
| (b) skip sink UpdateAggregates | ~430 ms | -6% |
| (c) local sink capacity 1<<22 (no abandon/repartition) | ~570–630 ms | about +30% |
| (d) no HLL / no adaptation | ~430 ms | at noise level |
| (e1) skip finalize Combine entirely | ~345 ms | -24% |
| (e2) source Scan emits nothing | ~460 ms | 0 |
| skip_lookups forced from the start | ~820–1100 ms | much worse |

Splitting the finalize Combine further:

| Finalize variant | Wall time | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| Scan only (no probe, no append) | ~340 ms | – |
| No CombineStates | ~458 ms | CombineStates costs about 0 |
| No append or InitializeStates (dummy row pointers) | ~385 ms | new-row materialisation costs about 70 ms (15%) |

That leaves the finalize probe at about 45 ms (10%).

Radix bits:

| Radix bits | Wall time | Change |
|---|---|---|
| Force 8, ignoring the row-width cap | ~440 ms | -3%, at noise level |
| 9 or 10 | ~600 ms | about +30% |

The only part over 8% is the finalize re-materialisation (about 15%). The fix for that is an in-place finalize, which E0002 already tried with no gain on q18. Even a perfect fix there is worth at most about 6% on q18, since the aggregate is only part of the query. I did not repeat it.
notes:
Dead ends, all measured:
- Growing local_sink_capacity (fewer abandons): +30%. A bigger thread-local table hurts cache more than the abandons cost, so the DecideAdaptation capacity rule should not be built.
- More radix bits (9 or 10): +30%. Forcing 8 bits by ignoring the row-width cap: -3%, noise.
- Forcing skip_lookups: much worse.
- HLL, source Scan and finalize CombineStates: each about 0.
- Skipping sink UpdateAggregates saves only 6%, so an InitializeStates/UpdateStates fast path has a ceiling of about 6% on the isolated aggregate, and less on q18.

Where the finalize Combine time goes: about 115 ms of the ~455 ms total. Of that, new-row append plus InitializeStates is about 70 ms and the probe into the partition table (~2 MB) is about 45 ms. The in-place finalize (E0002) is the only fix aimed at the append part; it already failed on q18.

Remaining sink time is about 225 ms (the ~340 ms scan-only-finalize run minus ~115 ms for the plain scan). It is spread across hashing, probing the local table, the partitioned append and the aggregate update, with no single dominant part.

Tooling tip: dbe-tool sql accepts several statements in one call, so `SET VARIABLE dbe_ablate=N; <query>; <query>...` works. Reading the flag through ClientConfig::GetUserVariable lets one build test many variants. Writing to /tmp is blocked.

Suggestion: the aggregate looks close to what this design can do for this shape. Later rounds may get more from other q18 operators: the 0.44 s and 0.24 s hash joins, and the orders scan at 0.32 s CPU.

title: Zonemap-prunable join key-set filter through compressed-materialization projections
summary:
I made two changes so a hash join with a small key set can skip row groups on its probe-side scans through zonemaps. On q18 the time went from 640.6 ms (current best) to 553.2 ms, which is -13.6%. That is from `dbe-tool bench q18` (quick check: 2 bindings, 4 hot runs each), and the results match.

(A) Join filters now pass through the integral compression projections. `JoinFilterPushdownColumn` has a new `Value storage_offset` field (null by default). `PushdownJoinFilterExpression` now accepts a `__internal_compress_integral_*(x, const)` call when x is integral and at most 64-bit, the constant is not null, and no offset has been set yet. It stores the constant and keeps going into x. The UNION rewrite copies the offset to each child. In `physical_hash_join.cpp`, a new helper `CastJoinFilterValueToStorage` turns each join key value v into the stored value: it adds v and the offset as HUGEINT (with an overflow check), then try-casts to the storage type. If any step fails, no filter is pushed. Both the min/max filters and the IN filter use it. The bloom filter is always skipped when an offset is set.

(B) Range-set filter. The IN-filter path now runs when the hash table holds at most 64 × `dynamic_or_filter_threshold` rows; the check is written so it cannot overflow. If the distinct keys still fit under the threshold, the IN filter is pushed exactly as before. If there are more and the storage type is integral (not UHUGEINT), the sorted keys are split at the (threshold−1) largest gaps. The result is pushed as an OptionalFilter of an OR of at most `threshold` inclusive ranges, so it is only used to skip row groups and never filters rows. A range holding one key becomes an equality. The existing NULL and dense-range bail-outs still apply, and the setting's default is unchanged.

From the profile: the lineitem probe scan now emits 17.5M of its 60M rows, and the orders scan emits 9.0M of 15M.
notes:
- **Optimizer order:** compressed materialization runs inside STATISTICS_PROPAGATION, which is after ROW_GROUP_PRUNER and TOP_N. Those two also call `GetPushdownFilterTargets`, but they never see compress expressions, so the new `storage_offset` cannot reach them.
- **Room for more:** with only 50 ranges over about 111 keys spread across the whole key range, about 70% of rows are skipped. Allowing more ranges than the threshold (checking a row group against them is cheap) would likely skip more, and lineitem scan time would fall further. That would need its own constant rather than reusing `dynamic_or_filter_threshold`.
- **Minor waste:** for non-integral keys above the threshold, the code still scans the keys before bailing out.
- **Not done:** the step-A-only check (`SET dynamic_or_filter_threshold=1000`) was skipped because A and B were built and measured together.

title: Extra selectivity for HAVING-style aggregate-result range filters in join ordering
summary:
The planned change alone did not flip the customer join. It was needed, but a second change was also needed. With both, q18 is 7–8% faster.

What I found: after adding the planned HAVING selectivity in relation_manager.cpp, EXPLAIN still showed customer on the build side and the semi join still estimated at about 3.5M rows. The reason is that the SEMI branch of CardinalityEstimator::CalculateUpdatedDenom never looks at the right side's size. It always estimates left / DEFAULT_SEMI_ANTI_SELECTIVITY (5), which gives orders 15M / ~4.25 ≈ 3.5M. So shrinking the subquery estimate had no effect.

Changes:
1. src/optimizer/join_order/relation_manager.cpp: a new static helper, FilterHasAggregateRangePredicate. It walks the datasource filters, including nested ANDs. It looks for a <, <=, > or >= comparison between a column of this aggregate's aggregate_index and a foldable expression. A column wrapped in a cast does not match. When found, the aggregate relation's estimate is multiplied by DEFAULT_SELECTIVITY (0.2) once more, never below 1. The aggregate's own SetEstimatedCardinality is unchanged.
2. src/optimizer/join_order/cardinality_estimator.cpp: for SEMI joins only, the selectivity is now max(DEFAULT_SEMI_ANTI_SELECTIVITY, tdom / rhs_cardinality). Here tdom is the join key domain and rhs_cardinality is the product of the estimates of the relations in the right set. It only applies when the right side is smaller than the domain. ANTI joins are unchanged.

Result: the plan in EXPLAIN now builds on the semi-joined orders side (about 214k estimated, 111 actual rows) and probes customer. The lineitem join still builds on the small side. Bench vs current best: 576.8 → 528.7 ms (-8.3%) on `bench q18`, and 563.2 → 521.6 ms (-7.4%) on a second run of the full visible set (q18 only). Results matched in both runs.
notes:
Both changes are needed. On its own, the HAVING selectivity has no effect on any semi-join plan, because the SEMI estimate ignores the right side's size. The SEMI estimate fix alone gives about 3M / 15M, which is equal to the default selectivity of 5, so the plan would not flip either.

The semi-estimate change is the larger lever and affects all semi joins with a small right side. That is broader than the issue planned, so the reviewer should look at it.

The lineitem join still gets its key-set dynamic filter: it showed up in the profile run with only the HAVING change, and the result checks still pass.

Possible follow-up: apply the same right-side-aware cap to MARK joins or to delim joins (relation_manager.cpp around line 546, which uses DEFAULT_SEMI_ANTI_SELECTIVITY).
